title: The coat and the dreams (Genesis 37:1–11)
hookLine: a favorite son, a colored coat, and brothers who can't speak peaceably

cards: Some family albums have one: the kid in the middle of every picture. The one whose drawings went on the fridge, whose birthday got the bigger cake, who got away with things. A sibling can still name that kid, years later.
Genesis has watched this pattern before. Isaac loved Esau more. Rebecca loved Jacob more.
Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah. Now Jacob, old, called Israel, has twelve sons, and he doesn't even try to hide his favorite.

teach.b: First, the favorite. Joseph is seventeen, the son of Rachel, the wife Jacob loved, born in Jacob's old age. He tends the flocks with his older half-brothers and brings his father a bad report about them.

In the Douay-Rheims: "Now Israel loved Joseph above all his sons, because he had him in his old age: and he made him a coat of divers colours. And his brethren seeing that he was loved by his father, more than all his sons, hated him, and could not speak peaceably to him."
Could not speak peaceably. Not even hello.

teach.h: A COAT THAT SAID: NOT LIKE YOU.
teach.b: Honestly, nobody is sure what that coat looked like. The Douay-Rheims, following the Latin, gives it many colors.

Some readers take the Hebrew, ketonet passim, as a long robe, the kind the second book of Samuel says a king's daughters wore. Either way, it wasn't work clothes. It said: this one doesn't do what you do.
Joseph dreams that his brothers' sheaves of grain bow down to his sheaf. Then that the sun, the moon and eleven stars bow down to him. And he tells them, both times.
The brothers hate him more. Even his father rebukes him: are your mother and I and your brothers to bow down to you? Last, the quiet line.
The brothers envied him, Genesis says, but his father kept the matter in mind.

teach.h: COULD NOT SPEAK PEACEABLY TO HIM.
teach.b: Catholics may hear an echo in Luke, where Mary keeps things and ponders them in her heart. The father who caused the trouble also senses something in it he can't yet see.

how: The Church reads the Joseph story in the weekday Mass during Lent, setting the brothers' envy beside the plot against Jesus in the Gospel.

o: a priest's robe worn for the sacrifice
Joseph's special coat, maybe a long robe
a shepherd's work cloak for the flocks

games.q: what's inside the coat story — tap the pairs.
p: the coat: many colors, or a long robe

s: scholars agree exactly what Joseph's coat looked like
the Douay-Rheims gives many colors; some read the Hebrew as a long robe. nobody is sure.
Joseph's brothers could not speak peaceably to him
the text says it plainly, because their father loved him above them all.
Joseph keeps his dreams to himself
he tells his brothers both times, and even his father rebukes him.

games.q: you're Joseph, seventeen. you've dreamed that your brothers' sheaves bowed down to yours. they already can't stand you. what do you do?
games.why: he tells them, and then tells them a second dream too. they hate him more, and even his father rebukes him, though he keeps the matter in mind.

practice: Think through the places you spend time, your family, your work, your parish, your friends, and notice where someone is treated as the favorite and someone else as the afterthought, without rushing to blame anyone.
Then look honestly at yourself: is there anyone you favor without meaning to, or anyone you overlook? If you pray, ask for a fairer heart.

wordCard.voice: Ketonet passim, Joseph's coat of many colors, the robe that said he didn't do what his brothers did, and set off their hatred. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: Joseph's coat. many colors in the Douay-Rheims; some read a long robe. the exact meaning is uncertain.

carryVoice: Your line: the coat caused trouble. A gift can say more than the giver means. Day three hundred sixty, done.
